content_items.title: Darwin Core Data Package: A Practical Evolution to Support Richer, Deeper, and New Biodiversity Data Sharing

programme.title: Darwin Core Data Package: A Practical Evolution to Support Richer, Deeper, and New Biodiversity Data Sharing
programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 2)
programme.abstract: After nearly two decades of success with Darwin Core and the Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A), the biodiversity informatics community faces the need to share data that are both richer in detail and deeper in structure than existing formats support. The Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) emerges as a direct response to this need—not as a replacement, but as a natural, practical evolution of a trusted standard. This presentation introduces DwC-DP as the result of six years of iterative, use case–driven development and testing, designed to extend the capabilities of Darwin Core without discarding its simplicity or adoption base.The journey began with the Unified Model—a comprehensive conceptual design proven to meet complex use cases, but too burdensome for everyday use. DwC-DP captures the “sweet spot” of that design: flexible enough to support emerging data types (e.g., Nucleotide Analyses, Organism Interactions, Survey Targets, Phylogenetic Trees), while retaining usability for current data publishers.Key features include modular schemas, a clearly event-based structure, and reusable extension patterns for concepts like Agent Roles, Media, Assertions, Protocols, and References. DwC-DP supports both flattened and nested forms, empowering users to adopt the level of complexity appropriate to their data.This talk will demystify DwC-DP for audiences ranging from cautious data providers to advanced integrators, highlighting its role as a community-informed technical foundation—supported by GBIF, governed by TDWG, and shaped by global feedback. Attendees will leave with a clearer sense of how DwC-DP enables more science and better decision-making without requiring a disruptive shift for those already using Darwin Core.

actual.identification_notes: Chair introduces 'John McCor' (ASR) for the overview; the speaker refers to himself as John ('when John has time to do it'), and programme context identifies John Wieczorek (affiliation from programme; not stated in captions). content_items.summary: John Wieczorek set out the place of the Darwin Core Data Package within Darwin Core. Proposed additions under review include a conceptual model (described as a first semantic layer for Darwin Core), new and changed terms, and a DwC-DP guide that mirrors the Darwin Core text guide behind Darwin Core Archives. Archives allow only one layer of connection and suit spreadsheets, whereas data packages allow arbitrary depth and suit relational databases; both rely on EML and CSV/TSV. New capabilities include separating occurrence events from collecting events, nesting of material, events and media, open-ended survey targets, user-defined agent roles, explicit organism interactions, assertions on anything, nucleotide analyses and declared controlled vocabularies. A bee-monitoring example contrasted a DwC-A "detective short story" with a DwC-DP "epic novel", stressing that publishers use only what they need. The talk ended with review timelines, commitments and resources, followed by Q&A on extended and digital specimens.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: DwC-DP is an additive, relational evolution of Darwin Core that keeps DwC-A working while allowing as much depth as a publisher needs.
content_items.why_it_matters: It frames the governance and design rationale for the whole symposium: why a new format rather than extending DwC-A, what is under public review, and what GBIF and TDWG commit to during the transition.

Why something new: changing DwC-A would break current practice, and DwC-A uses a home-grown technology, whereas Frictionless Data Packages align with the wider world.
Bee-monitoring example: field identification, specimen, DNA sequence — three identifications that may disagree — plus assertions, media, bibliographic references and agents.
Public review began mid-September 2025 and runs at least until mid-December, possibly longer depending on consensus.

Commitments: continued support and training for DwC-A; augmented support for DwC-DP; IPT and the Metabarcoding Data Toolkit already publish DwC-DP in testing; a data mapping guide; example datasets; a community-produced user guide in progress.
After ratification, schemas go to the Darwin Core Maintenance Group, with hoped-for quarterly releases from 2026.

content_items.title: Two Decades of ABCD: Advancing Structured Biodiversity Data Sharing

programme.title: Two Decades of ABCD: Advancing Structured Biodiversity Data Sharing

speakers.name: Anton Güntsch
speakers.affiliation: Freie Universität Berlin, Botanic Garden and Botanical Museum Berlin

programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 2)
programme.abstract: ABCD (Access to Biological Collection Data, https:||abcd.tdwg.org|) is a TDWG (Biodiversity Information Standards) standard that was developed by a broad international collaboration to create a structured framework for capturing and exchanging biodiversity data.ABCD was implemented as a hierarchical XML schema, allowing it to interoperate seamlessly with standardized software components. This design enables diverse applications such as data publication, harvesting and aggregation, quality control, and access through data portals. By facilitating harmonized exchange and integration of primary biodiversity data, ABCD supports robust scientific workflows and analyses (Holetschek et al. 2012, https:||doi.org|10.1080|11263504.2012.740085).Over the past two decades, ABCD has undergone continuous refinement to align with the evolving needs of the biodiversity informatics community. In parallel with the widely used Darwin Core standard (Wieczorek et al. 2012, https:||doi.org|10.1371|journal.pone.0029715), ABCD plays a vital role in promoting the harmonization, mobilization, and dissemination of biodiversity data across both national and international infrastructures. Domain-specific extensions for ABCD play a central role for special-interest networks, like the Global Genome Biodiversity Network (GGBN, Droege et al. 2016, https:||doi.org|10.1093|database|baw125). An important example of the use of ABCD at the national level is the establishment of standardized data flows between domain data centers and central aggregation and data analysis platforms in NFDI4Biodiversity in Germany (Glöckner et al. 2020, https:||doi.org|10.5281|zenodo.3943645).The latest iteration of the standard, ABCD version 3.0, introduces a significant architectural enhancement: the semantic definitions of data elements are now decoupled from their structural representation in XML. This modularization promotes greater flexibility in how the standard can be applied and reused, facilitating integration into emerging data ecosystems and enhancing interoperability (Fichtmueller et al. 2019, https:||doi.org|10.3897|biss.3.37214). In particular, ABCD contributes to the emerging "Darwin Core Data Package" a new initiative aimed at enabling the global exchange and reuse of structured collection and observational data based on Frictionless Data technology (https:||frictionlessdata.io|).

speakers.affiliation: Freie Universität Berlin, Botanic Garden and Botanical Museum Berlin

content_items.summary: Anton Güntsch traced the history of biodiversity data models. About 30 years ago, comprehensive relational reference models (e.g. Walter Berendsohn's model for collections and surveys) were used mainly for local databases, while early networks such as the Species Analyst (Z39.50) and the European natural history specimen information network used much simpler models. XML was then agreed as the right balance of comprehensibility and expressiveness. That led to ABCD, developed between 2001 and 2006: comprehensive, highly hierarchical, with extension slots for networks such as GGBN, and now about 100 provider installations, more than 10 special-interest networks, integration into GBIF, and use in NFDI4Biodiversity. ABCD 3.0 made it a semantic standard. Güntsch argued that DwC-DP's relational structure realises the original relational vision. The ABCD/BioCASe community will help develop and maintain DwC-DP, build templates, and extend the BioCASe help desk to complex DwC-DP data.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: For the ABCD/BioCASe community, DwC-DP fulfils the long-held aim of exchanging relational biodiversity data, and they will actively support it.
content_items.why_it_matters: It places DwC-DP in a 30-year lineage of biodiversity data models and commits a major existing standard community and its help desk to supporting the transition rather than competing with it.
key_points: Around 30 years ago the community built comprehensive relational reference models for collections and surveys, used mainly for isolated local databases.
Early network pilots used simplified models: the Species Analyst (Z39.50) and the European natural history specimen information network (HTTP, XML with a common DTD).
These pilots led to agreement that XML offered the right balance of comprehensibility and expressiveness, the basis for ABCD.

ABCD was developed 2001–2006 by an international team; it is comprehensive, highly hierarchical, has few controlled vocabularies, has extension slots for networks like GGBN, and supports structured annotations.
The version history is described as messy; the main versions are ABCD 2.06 (most widely used), 2.1 and 3.0 (semantic).
Infrastructure includes provider software, harvesting and indexing tools, portal software and monitoring components.
About 100 ABCD provider installations worldwide, over 10 special-interest networks, integration into GBIF and use within NFDI4Biodiversity; a BioCASe help desk supports providers.
ABCD serves as a container for other standards: geosciences, DNA and anthropological extensions.
DwC-DP's relational structure closely resembles the early relational models.
The ABCD/BioCASe initiative will contribute to DwC-DP development and maintenance, develop templates for typical usage scenarios, and extend the help desk to DwC-DP.

content_items.title: Seamless Integration: How DiSSCo's openDS Facilitates Data Interoperability with the Darwin Core Data Package

programme.title: Seamless Integration: How DiSSCo's openDS Facilitates Data Interoperability with the Darwin Core Data Package
programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 2)
programme.abstract: The Distributed System for Scientific Collection (DiSSCo) has been following the developments of the Darwin Core Conceptual Model and the Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) with great interest. DiSSCo is an emerging European Research Infrastructure Consortium (ERIC) aimed at accelerating the digitisation of Europe's Natural History Collections. Vital to this acceleration is the exchange of knowledge, ideas, and tools, which can be done through the DiSSCo infrastructure. Essential for the infrastructure is a collective language in the form of data standards, which we call open Digital Specimen (openDS).The development of openDS has been done in parallel to the development of the Darwin Core Conceptual Model. OpenDS has reached production maturity after it has gone through a public review in 2024. OpenDS is a document focussed specification optimized for data curation, where each document represents a Fair Digital Object (FDO). This means that openDS is broader than the specimen information but also contains models to capture annotations and provenance. As the openDS Digital Specimen and Digital Media models are developed on top of existing TDWG standards and the work on the Darwin Core Conceptual Model, they can be seen as an implementation of the conceptual model. Translations between openDS and DwC-DP, both implementations of the conceptual model, can therefore be made without any loss in data.During the session, DiSSCo will share their experience with implementing both the conceptual model in the form of openDS and the translation from openDS to the DwC-DP. DiSSCo will be able to create DwC-DP for any of their data, showing how specimen from Natural History Collections can be mapped to DwC-DP.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded virtual presentation as scheduled; the chair says Sam Leeflang (ASR 'Sam Lupang'; self-introduction ASR 'Sam Leang') could not attend in person and was online to answer questions in the chat. ASR: 'Disco' = DiSSCo; 'open DS'/'opens' = openDS; 'FDOS' = FDOs (FAIR Digital Objects); 'John Courage' = John Wieczorek; 'GBF unified model' = GBIF Unified Model; 'civilization structure' = serialisation structure; 'nuclide' = nucleotide; 'Dharma habitat' = probably the Darwin Core term habitat. In Part 1, Tim Robertson previewed this talk when answering a question on extended specimens (see livingdata-2025-dp-p1-07-discussion).

content_items.summary: Sam Leeflang explained that DiSSCo aims to create FAIR Digital Objects as digital extended specimens. In 2022, rather than invent yet another standard, DiSSCo chose to align its open Digital Specimen (openDS) specification with the GBIF Unified Model, and later with the Darwin Core conceptual model. openDS went through public review and is now in production. It is described as a separate, specimen-specific implementation of the conceptual model: document-oriented, denormalised JSON optimised for mutating single specimens. DwC-DP, in contrast, is a full, normalised tabular reference implementation. DiSSCo mapped almost all openDS terms to about 23 DwC-DP schemas, and any dataset in its acceptance environment can now be downloaded as a DwC-A or DwC-DP (the largest about 750,000 records). Identifiers implicit in nested documents had to be created with MD5 hashes and temporary tables.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Because openDS was built on the same conceptual model, DiSSCo can transform specimen data to DwC-DP with almost no loss, needing only generated identifiers.
content_items.why_it_matters: It shows that two different serialisations of the Darwin Core conceptual model — document-oriented for curation and tabular for transport — can interoperate nearly losslessly, supporting the case that the conceptual model works as a common language.
key_points: DiSSCo (Distributed System of Scientific Collections) aims to accelerate digitisation of European specimen data as rich FAIR Digital Objects (digital extended specimens).
In 2022 there was no standard to reuse; to avoid adding another competing standard, DiSSCo aligned with the GBIF Unified Model presented by John Wieczorek and Tim Robertson.
openDS moved through public review last year and is used in production.
openDS is considered a separate, specimen-specific implementation of the Darwin Core conceptual model; DwC-DP is seen as a full reference implementation.

openDS does not implement all classes (e.g. no nucleotide analysis or sequence) and uses a document-oriented JSON structure that denormalises and duplicates information per specimen, because DiSSCo expects many mutations on single specimens.
Expected benefits of alignment: a common data and human language, leveraging TDWG community work, and lossless transfer from openDS to DwC-DP as a transport model.
Implementation: about 23 schemas, almost all openDS terms mapped in the acceptance environment; any dataset downloadable as DwC-A or DwC-DP; largest DwC-DP about 750,000 records.
Material is at the centre of both the openDS model and the DwC-DP implementation.
Lesson: interoperability is good with little data loss, but relationships implicit in nested documents required generated identifiers (MD5 hash of the object), temporary tables and CSV dumps.
After ratification, DiSSCo will move DwC-DP export to production and move future openDS iterations closer to the conceptual model, including collaboration on controlled vocabularies.

content_items.title: Implementation Status of the Darwin Core Data Package (DwC DP) at GBIF

programme.title: Implementation Status of the Darwin Core Data Package (DwC DP) at GBIF
programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 2)
programme.abstract: The implementation of the Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) goes beyond enabling publishing mechanisms,i t also benefits from data services that support search, discovery, and exploration. GBIF.org currently offers a robust data indexing platform, including an API and data portal. A large proportion of the available data has been published using the existing Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A) standard. While DwC-A’s simplicity has enabled effective aggregation within a centralized infrastructure, the richer modeling capabilities of the new DwC-DP introduce both opportunities and challenges for future data services.To address this, the GBIF Secretariat is developing a phased roadmap for data ingestion and discovery services based on the new DwC-DP. The roadmap includes: enabling the publishing and registration of DwC-DP datasets; extending dataset catalogs to support discovery; facilitating exploration of dataset structures and schemas; and, in the near future, implementing global data services for cross-dataset querying and downloads, comparable to those currently available on GBIF.org.This presentation provides a status update on the development of this roadmap. It demonstrates how a DwC-DP dataset can be published, ingested, and explored through its internal structure via a test data portal. Finally, it outlines upcoming service enhancements for both the current DwC-A platform and the evolving DwC-DP based infrastructure.

content_items.summary: Federico Méndez gave GBIF's DwC-DP implementation plan. It has four areas: standards promotion and support, data publishing, dataset representation in the GBIF platform/APIs/portal, and longer-term data services. For the coming year there are three milestones. Milestone 1 covers provisional support in the IPT and Metabarcoding Data Toolkit, validation tools, and a minimal dataset view on the new GBIF website before year end. Milestone 2 covers mature documentation, IPT mapping UX, a versioning strategy, DwC-A/DwC-DP conversion and improved dataset pages. Milestone 3 covers long-term questions such as new data services and whether one or several portals are needed. A development-environment demo showed an MDT-published DwC-DP registered in GBIF, with a graphical view of tables, fields and relationships and basic table exploration. Planned additions include a DwC-DP download format, maps, metrics, validation reports and an API. In Q&A, Méndez said milestones 1 and 2 are not sequential.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: GBIF is phasing in DwC-DP support, from provisional publishing and dataset views now to integrated data services later, with publishing and display developed in parallel.
content_items.why_it_matters: It tells publishers and data users concretely what GBIF will support and when, and what remains undecided (e.g. new data services and portals) for richer DwC-DP data.
key_points: Four implementation areas: data standards promotion and support; data publishing; representation of DwC-DP datasets in the GBIF platform, APIs and portal; data services (long-term).
Three milestones for the coming year.

Milestone 1: schema and standards work, provisional support in the IPT and MDT, validation and mapping tools (also as GBIF portal services), and minimal display of DwC-DP datasets in the new GBIF website before year end.

Milestone 2: mature technical and user documentation, improve IPT mapping UX, initiate a versioning strategy for progressive improvements, tools for conversion between DwC-A and DwC-DP, improved dataset representation.
Milestone 3 (future): new data services, the question of one versus multiple data portals for very different kinds of datasets, multiple APIs.

Demo (development environment): MDT exports DwC-A or DwC-DP; a registered DwC-DP is shown as a graphical view of the data package descriptor (tables, fields, relationships), with basic exploration of the event and other tables.
Planned features: DwC-DP download format, map view where coordinates exist, table and column metrics, validation status reports, and a basic API.
Libraries: a Java library to validate and read data packages, and a library to load data packages into data stores (probably Elasticsearch, Postgres and ClickHouse).
Q&A: milestones 1 and 2 are not sequential, so users can publish soon with a way to view datasets and better documentation.

content_items.title: Implementing the proposed DwC-DP format in GBIF: data publishing tools

programme.title: Implementing the proposed DwC-DP format in GBIF: data publishing tools
programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 2)
programme.abstract: The GBIF Integrated Publishing Toolkit (IPT) has enabled the publication of thousands of datasets in a robust and user-friendly way for more than a decade. This success is due in part to the simplicity and clarity of the Darwin Core standard, as well as the straightforward workflows the IPT provides for data publishers.As the data model supporting the mobilization of more complex biodiversity data evolves, so too must the infrastructure. Traditional schemas like Darwin Core have served the community well, but they limit the expression of richer biodiversity information. To address this, GBIF is working towards introducing the new Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP), designed to better represent complex relationships among biodiversity entities. While DwC-DP opens exciting possibilities for linking entities and supporting diverse data types, it also presents significant challenges for developers and data publishers. We must balance this increased richness with usability, ensuring that tools like the IPT remain accessible to a broad community. Key challenges include managing data model versions, providing user guidance for complex schemas, and ensuring that schema governance and validation workflows are transparent and sustainable.This presentation will offer a vision for implementing DwC-DP support in the IPT, including design decisions, current state and limitations, and planned improvements.We aim to inspire contributions and ideas from the TDWG community to improve tooling and practices, ultimately helping to lower the barriers to publishing high-quality, richly structured biodiversity datasets.

actual.identification_notes: Self-introduces as 'Mikail', lead developer for the IPT at GBIF ('JBIF'); chair says 'Male Podski Podski' (ASR); also referred to as 'Mika' by Federico Méndez and 'Misha' by an audience member. ASR: 'IP'/'AP' = IPT; 'OBS' = OBIS; 'pentological' = paleontological; 'Daring'/'diving core' = Darwin Core. The question taken immediately after this talk was addressed to Federico Méndez and is attached to livingdata-2025-dp-p2-04-gbif-implementation. A later question to Mikhail about community dataset profiles is in the general discussion (livingdata-2025-dp-p2-07-discussion).

content_items.summary: Mikhail Podolskiy, lead developer of GBIF's Integrated Publishing Toolkit (IPT), discussed the user-interface challenges of supporting DwC-DP: a large, overwhelming new model, many identifiers and join tables, and identifier maintenance. A dropdown listing all 70-plus tables clearly does not scale. Proposed solutions were profiles or templates: subsets of the model with selected tables and fields, descriptions and search keywords, which can be public or local and are managed within the IPT. A made-up paleontological profile was shown as an example. Other ideas were table categories, an improved dropdown, an advanced search across fields, examples and descriptions (e.g. for 'collector'), a schematic visualisation of mapped tables like the one in the MDT, and 'splitting tools' that break a flat source table into several DwC-DP tables and generate their identifiers.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: To keep DwC-DP publishable in the IPT, GBIF proposes profiles, better model navigation and search, visualisation, and tools that split tables and generate identifiers.
content_items.why_it_matters: Usability of publishing tools is likely to decide whether DwC-DP is adopted; this sets out how the most widely used GBIF publishing tool intends to make a 70-plus-table model manageable.
key_points: The IPT is a formatting and sharing tool for publishing to GBIF and OBIS.

A profile management tool in the IPT would be needed to edit, add fields and tables, save, upload and download profiles.
Navigation ideas: table categories, improved dropdown lists, and an advanced search engine across tables, terms, examples and descriptions.
Visualisation: a schematic view of mapped tables and their connections, as already implemented in the MDT.
Splitting tools: split source data (e.g. event ID, date, collector) into multiple DwC-DP tables and generate the required identifiers automatically.

content_items.title: Darwin Core Data Package public review process

programme.title: Darwin Core Data Package public review process
programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 2)
programme.abstract: The TDWG Vocabulary Maintenance Specification (VMS, http:||rs.tdwg.org|vms|doc|specification|) provides a mechanism for making a set of coordinated changes to a vocabulary. The Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) falls into this category of coordinated additions to the Darwin Core standard (http:||www.tdwg.org|standards|450). In this presentation, I will describe how the public review process described by the VMS applies to the DwC-DP proposal. Specifically, I will detail: what is under review, how the proposed changes will be added to the standard and its documentation, and how the public can provide comments to participate in the public review.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded virtual presentation as scheduled. Self-introduction captioned 'Steve Baskoff, the convenor of the Darwin Core Maintenance Group'; chair says 'Steve Basco'. ASR: 'Tadwig'/'TAWIG' = TDWG; 'Dolan core'/'dollar core' = Darwin Core. Questions about the review process were handled in the general discussion (livingdata-2025-dp-p2-07-discussion), where the chair also relayed the speaker's chat reply.

content_items.summary: Steve Baskauf, convenor of the Darwin Core Maintenance Group, explained how the DwC-DP proposal is being reviewed under the TDWG Vocabulary Maintenance Specification. Anyone may propose changes; the maintenance group assesses demand, efficacy and stability, then opens a public comment period seeking consensus, and the Executive Committee ratifies. Because DwC-DP is a vocabulary enhancement beyond the basic term layer, it required user feedback documents. Under review are two documents, the conceptual model and the data package guide (based on Frictionless Data Packages), plus related term additions and changes. Implementation details such as how data packages are actually built are outside the standard. The review opened in September and runs at least until 16 December: 90 days instead of the usual 30 because of the proposal's complexity. Comments go to GitHub issues, reached via a landing page and per-class issue summaries, or by email to the convenor.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: The DwC-DP proposal is in an extended 90-day TDWG public review covering the conceptual model, the data package guide and related term changes, with comments taken on GitHub or by email.
content_items.why_it_matters: It tells the community exactly what is up for decision, what is not, and how to take part, which is essential for reaching the consensus needed to ratify DwC-DP.
key_points: Changes to TDWG vocabularies are governed by the Vocabulary Maintenance Specification.
Any person or group may propose changes; the maintenance group reviews proposals for community demand, efficacy and stability of existing implementations.
Approved proposals normally get a 30-day public comment period seeking consensus; the Executive Committee checks procedures and ratifies.
Vocabulary enhancements (beyond the 'bag of terms' layer) require user feedback documents.
Under review: the conceptual model document, the data package guide (based on Frictionless Data Packages), and term additions/modifications needed to impose this structure.
Darwin Core data packages will implement the data packages guide as DwC-As implement the text guide, but the implementation details are outside the standard and not part of the review.
A landing page (linked from the TDWG website news item) gives document links, term changes and per-class issue summaries.
The maintenance group approved the proposal for public comment in September; review runs at least to December 16 (90 days).
Comments are made in the Darwin Core GitHub issue tracker or emailed to the convenor to post.
End users need not feel bad about not commenting on the documents, which mainly target application developers; there will be later opportunities as implementations develop.

methods: TDWG public review and consensus process

notable_claims.claim: The maintenance group reviews proposals against three criteria: community demand, efficacy in meeting an identified need, and maintaining stability of existing implementations.
Vocabulary enhancements require user feedback documents to be submitted with the proposal.
Implementation details of Darwin Core data packages are outside the standard and not part of the review.
The public review is ongoing until at least December 16th and lasts 90 days rather than the normal 30 because of the proposal's complexity.
Commenters who have difficulty with GitHub can email their comments to the convenor, who will post them.

recommendations: Review the term changes grouped by class using the issue summaries.
Participate in the review via the GitHub issue tracker or by email.
future_work: Additional opportunities for user feedback as implementations based on the new documents are developed.

representative_excerpt.text: The public review is ongoing until at least December 16th. This period of review is 90 days rather than the normal 30 days due to the complexity of the proposal.

actual.identification_notes: General Q&A after the final talk, matching the scheduled Part 2 Discussion. Tim Robertson re-introduces himself at 01:17:09.760. Several answers are unattributed in the captions; those attributed to John Wieczorek (review participation, nested assertions, expert forum — he says 'instead of just me' and offers to be available for the next year — and the project class) are inferred from content and should be checked. The person who described the user guide at 01:16:40.159 is unidentified. 'Erica Criminal' (ASR) = Erica Krimmel. 'Misha' = Mikhail Podolskiy. 'Fede' = Federico Méndez. Questions about the review process relate to Steve Baskauf's talk, and the profiles question relates to Mikhail Podolskiy's talk, but they are kept here because they were asked and answered by the panel in the general Q&A and the threads cross-reference one another.

content_items.summary: The closing discussion began with whether the public review receives adequate comments. The panel feared the community is not yet educated enough to comment meaningfully on such a complex, interdependent proposal, where a lack of consensus on one part could cascade. Issue summaries let people focus on what matters to them, Erica Krimmel had volunteered to host 'Darwin Core hours', and GitHub thumbs-up reactions are a useful way to signal agreement. A suggestion that thematic communities propose and endorse IPT dataset profiles led Tim Robertson to recount how community-specific publishing models (ColDP, Camtrap DP) were dropped after fragmentation concerns, only for profiles to re-emerge as the unified model felt overwhelming. Tim also said metabarcoding DwC-As reach half a terabyte because of star-schema repetition, and DwC-DP can shrink them about a thousandfold. Other questions covered nested trait assertions (not supported; would need a new term), a forum for unusual use cases, project-level metadata (no project class yet), and building expertise through training and the TDWG review.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Panellists acknowledged that review participation, model complexity and expertise are real constraints, while arguing that metabarcoding scale makes something like DwC-DP operationally necessary.
content_items.why_it_matters: The discussion reveals open design gaps (recursive assertions, project class), governance risks in the review, and the operational driver (metabarcoding data volume) behind GBIF's implementation priorities.
key_points: Review participation: fair so far but uneven; the community may not be educated enough to comment meaningfully; no consensus means a proposal is excluded, and interdependencies could cascade.
Issue summaries were a new way of organising issues so that interested people can go directly to the parts that matter to them.
Erica Krimmel had volunteered to host 'Darwin Core hours' for education and discussion (not yet scheduled).
GitHub thumbs-up reactions are the built-in way to signal agreement without flooding issues with comments.
Steve Baskauf replied in the chat (relayed by the chair) that the number of comments depends on the topic.
Dataset profiles: GBIF would implement the concept and communities would decide on and manage their own profiles; the user guide aims to give domain-specific starting points.

Tim Robertson: community-specific publishing models (ColDP for checklists, Camtrap DP) were discouraged as fragmenting; a single model became overwhelming; simplified profiles may return, integrable through the conceptual model.
Metabarcoding DwC-As with about 27 million detections reach half a terabyte due to star-schema repetition; the same data as DwC-DP via the MDT can be about a thousand times smaller.
GBIF may need to implement part of DwC-DP specifically to support metabarcoding even if not everything at once.
No recursive relationship on assertions yet for nested trait measurements; a workaround exists but a related-assertion identifier term could be added given a strong use case.
Model experts have been helping with unusual use cases for over a year and will continue; the goal is to produce more experts.
No project class yet; project information is limited to EML or project names/IDs in provenance; a project class could be developed.
Building expertise: an internal GBIF node-manager training (correcting the Part 1 workshop answer), bringing the work to TDWG, keeping the community together; training materials are freely available.

nested and recursive assertions for traits
expert support for unusual use cases

notable_claims.claim: When consensus is not achieved in a Darwin Core review the proposal is not included, and with DwC-DP's interdependencies a failure on one part could cause a cascade.
Thumbs-up reactions on GitHub issues are the built-in way to signal agreement and are useful feedback.
Strong feedback discouraged community-specific publishing models because they could fragment the community.
Metabarcoding Darwin Core Archives with around 27 million detections are about half a terabyte because of star-schema repetition.
The same input data published as DwC-DP through the Metabarcoding Data Toolkit can be about a thousand times smaller.
There is currently no recursive relationship on assertions; one could be added with a new related-assertion identifier term if there is a strong use case.
There is currently no project class in DwC-DP; project information is limited to EML or project names and IDs in provenance.
The GBIF DwC-DP training was an internal event for GBIF node managers, correcting an earlier statement in Part 1.

recommendations: Use thumbs-up reactions on GitHub issues to indicate agreement.
Bring strong use cases (e.g. for nested assertions or a project class) to the model maintainers.

Community expertise to review and implement the model is limited.

Possible project class.
Darwin Core hours hosted by Erica Krimmel.
Continued expert support for use cases for at least the next year.

Mean and standard deviation assertions linked through the assertion-type vocabulary.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Unattributed (probably John Wieczorek): a big worry for this complex proposal; simpler reviews get plenty of interaction, but complex topics can fail to reach consensus, and interdependencies could cascade; the community may not be educated enough; issue summaries help people focus; participation so far is fair. Another speaker noted Erica Krimmel volunteered to host Darwin Core hours. Later the chair relayed Steve Baskauf's chat reply that comment numbers depend on the topic.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Mikhail Podolskiy: GBIF would implement the profile concept and communities would decide and manage their own profiles. q_and_a.answer_summary: Unattributed (probably John Wieczorek): no recursive relationship on assertions; it was considered but lacked a strong use case; a workaround is possible but unclear; adding a related-assertion ID term would be simple — bring a good use case.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Unattributed (probably John Wieczorek): this has been done for over a year and will continue; the hope is to produce more experts, and the answerer will be available to help for at least the next year.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Unattributed (probably John Wieczorek): a project class was investigated but not implemented for lack of a use case; GBIF sees demand; currently only EML or project names/IDs in provenance; a project class can be developed.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Tim Robertson: by sharing the work at this conference and bringing it to TDWG; GBIF held an internal training for node managers (correcting an earlier statement) to build capacity that can spread to their communities; the community must be kept together; ideas are welcome.
